projects.rationale: Strong on open access (partial open-source, no paywalls) and direct practitioner benefit (serves grassroots activists not institutions), but lacks clear evidence of platform independence or anti-surveillance design in the dossier.

While open source (AGPL-3.0) and free to use, the platform primarily serves municipal governments and public administrations rather than individual practitioners, and depends on a single foundation's sustainability without clear anti-extraction measures.

While the project provides open educational resources (partial open source, no paywall), it primarily serves well-resourced institutions and researchers in AI safety rather than marginalized practitioners, and lacks evidence of anti-extraction design or platform independence.

Alaveteli exemplifies Frederick's values by providing free, open-source infrastructure that empowers individual citizens and journalists to directly access government information, bypassing institutional gatekeepers while maintaining independence from corporate platforms.

While Aleph provides free, open-source investigative tools directly to journalists and activists (strong on criteria 1-2), its heavy dependence on US government funding with veto powers over appointments fundamentally compromises the anti-extraction and independence criterion.

AlgorithmWatch scores moderately as a nonprofit watchdog organization that provides some open research and tools, but primarily serves institutional actors (policymakers, EU bodies) rather than directly empowering individual practitioners, while remaining grant-dependent on government and foundation funding rather than achieving platform independence.

Open-source platform serving citizens directly scores well on access and practitioner benefit, but lacks evidence of anti-extraction design and has documented government partnerships that may compromise independence.

While the guide provides free access to information (partial credit for Criterion 1), it primarily serves already-empowered technologists and policymakers rather than marginalized practitioners, and operates within existing institutional frameworks rather than challenging extractive platforms.

Anna's Archive exemplifies Frederick's values through radical open access to knowledge (bypassing paywalls), direct benefit to students/researchers over publishers, and explicit anti-extraction stance against corporate academic publishing monopolies, though legal vulnerabilities and limited governance transparency prevent a perfect score.
Open-source database documenting landlord surveillance tech directly serves tenants against extractive platforms, though limited evidence of removing access barriers beyond information provision.

While Aragon provides open-source DAO governance tools, it primarily serves well-resourced blockchain protocols and token holders rather than marginalized communities, and its VC funding model and blockchain dependency contradict Frederick's anti-extraction and platform independence principles.

arXiv exemplifies free and open access to scholarly knowledge, directly serves individual researchers and students globally while bypassing commercial publishers, though partial Cornell University hosting and reliance on institutional funding prevent a perfect anti-extraction score.

Academic theoretical framework paper that serves platform operators and researchers rather than direct practitioners, lacks open source implementation, and appears to strengthen platform governance rather than reduce platform dependence.

Strong alignment across all criteria: open-source surveillance transparency tool serving journalists and communities against extractive surveillance infrastructure, though partial open-source status and EFF dependency prevent maximum score.

Strong on open access (MIT licensed, free toolkit) and practitioner benefit (serves individual journalists/researchers), but corporate foundation funding and lack of explicit anti-surveillance stance limit the anti-extraction score.
Strong on practitioner benefit (helping low-income households access benefits) and free access, but government partnership with DWP and lack of open source limit anti-extraction score.

While SlopStop addresses information quality through community-driven AI content detection, it operates within a paid subscription model ($10-25/month for Kagi), serves primarily existing Kagi subscribers rather than removing access barriers, and strengthens a commercial search platform rather than empowering individual practitioners or communities.

Strong alignment on open access (AGPL-3.0, self-hostable) and community benefit (cooperatives, activists), with explicit anti-extraction design (federated, no VC funding), though early-stage adoption limits impact evidence.

While Bluesky offers partial open-source components and claims decentralization, it remains a VC-funded platform with centralized control that primarily benefits the platform itself rather than individual practitioners, failing to meet Frederick's core criteria of genuine open access and anti-extraction design.
Open-source platform enabling community ownership scores well on access and anti-extraction, but serves organizations alongside individual practitioners, limiting its practitioner-first impact.

While serving charity sector practitioners, the project lacks open access (no open source, survey data not publicly available), primarily benefits organizations over individual practitioners, and shows no evidence of platform independence or anti-extraction design.

While partially open-source and serving web3 communities, CharmVerse operates as a VC-funded platform with subscription model that primarily benefits already-resourced blockchain organizations rather than removing barriers for individual practitioners or marginalized communities.

While the tool provides free access to licensing guidance and serves individual developers, its GitHub ownership and lack of anti-extraction measures limit its alignment with the evaluator's emphasis on platform independence and practitioner empowerment.

Strong open-source participation platform (GitHub verified, MIT license implied) that directly serves communities and NGOs for democratic decision-making, though government partnerships and institutional focus temper the anti-extraction stance.

Mixed performance: strong on open access (partial open source, GitHub presence) but primarily serves organizations and governments rather than individual practitioners, with unclear platform independence given reliance on international grant funding.

CiviClick scores poorly as a closed-source, subscription-based platform serving well-resourced organizations (companies, agencies, associations) rather than individual practitioners or communities, with no evidence of removing access barriers or platform independence.

Closed-source platform connecting citizens to civic opportunities lacks evidence of removing access barriers, appears to serve as intermediary rather than direct practitioner benefit, and shows no anti-extraction design principles.

Open-source civic infrastructure that routes transparency benefits directly to citizens while bypassing commercial intermediaries, though early-stage status and limited deployment evidence constrain the score.

Strong on open access (open source, no paywalls) and practitioner benefit (serves nonprofits/NGOs directly), but moderate on anti-extraction due to CMS dependencies and lack of explicit platform independence architecture.

While the platform provides free access to information about civic tech projects, it primarily serves as a directory rather than providing direct tools to practitioners, and its institutional partnerships and grant funding model suggest it operates more as an intermediary resource hub than a direct empowerment tool for communities.

CKAN scores moderately as an open-source data management system that enables government transparency but primarily serves institutional needs rather than direct practitioner empowerment, with mixed independence from corporate infrastructure.

Scores well on open access (GitHub presence, volunteer-driven) and practitioner focus (tech workers self-organizing), but lacks evidence of platform independence and shows dependency on Slack infrastructure.

Open-source participatory budgeting tool serving community organizations scores well on access (MIT license, free) and practitioner benefit, but lacks evidence of anti-extraction design and primarily serves already-organized groups rather than removing fundamental barriers.

A closed-source, VC-funded platform that serves cryptocurrency communities through token-gating, reinforcing platform dependence rather than enabling practitioner independence or removing access barriers.

A guidebook for collaborative data maintenance that partially meets open access criteria but primarily serves organizations rather than individual practitioners and lacks clear anti-extraction stance.

Strong on free access (no paywall) and direct practitioner benefit (serves activists not institutions), but lacks open source commitment and relies on centralized platform architecture rather than distributed alternatives.

While serving community members and local governments with open methodology, the project lacks open source implementation, primarily benefits institutional actors through government partnerships, and shows no evidence of platform independence or anti-extraction design.

Strong alignment on open access (MIT licensed, free toolkit) and community benefit (serves organizers directly, not institutions), but unclear on platform independence given partnerships with government innovation labs and major foundation funding.

Project provides free access to political funding data serving journalists and citizens directly, but lacks open source code and appears to be a simple data aggregation without challenging extractive intermediaries.

Strong on open access (open source, free database) and serving practitioners/citizens directly, but limited anti-extraction stance as it primarily aggregates existing government documents without challenging surveillance infrastructure.

CONSUL Democracy scores well on free/open access (fully open source, MIT-style license) and anti-extraction stance (government-hosted, no corporate intermediaries), but scores moderately on practitioner benefit as it primarily serves government institutions rather than directly empowering individual practitioners or communities.

While open source and promoting transparency in data governance, this project primarily serves institutional actors (government agencies, researchers, private sector organizations) rather than individual practitioners, and strengthens rather than bypasses institutional data infrastructure.
A cooperative network that embodies practitioner-first values and platform independence, though limited evidence prevents assessment of actual open access implementation.

Open source commenting platform scores well on free access (Apache 2.0, GitHub) and practitioner benefit (serves journalists/newsrooms directly), but loses points for corporate platform dependencies and funding from major media institutions rather than full independence.

While Cortico amplifies underheard voices through small-group dialogue, it fails all three criteria: it's a closed-source platform (not open access), primarily serves institutional clients like government agencies and foundations (not direct practitioner benefit), and operates within rather than against existing institutional structures.

While COTSI provides valuable research infrastructure for tracking digital manipulation, it fails all three core criteria: it's not open source or freely accessible, it primarily serves institutional researchers rather than direct practitioners, and it operates within rather than against surveillance infrastructure.

Creative Commons scores highly on all three criteria: providing free legal tools that remove copyright barriers (C1), directly benefiting individual creators and educators rather than platforms (C2), and maintaining independence from corporate surveillance infrastructure while enabling decentralized sharing (C3).

While the project maintains open-source tools and research, it primarily serves institutional actors (policymakers, regulators, tech companies) rather than individual practitioners, and operates within existing platform governance structures rather than providing alternatives to them.

While HDX provides open data access for humanitarian purposes, it primarily serves institutional actors (UN agencies, large NGOs) rather than individual practitioners, and operates within rather than challenging existing power structures.

Strong alignment on free access (open source, APIs) and practitioner benefit (serves journalists, researchers, citizens directly), but government partnerships and institutional funding model prevent full anti-extraction score.
Strong alignment with open access and community benefit principles, but early-stage project with unproven sustainability model and Mozilla Foundation dependency limits score.

While the project aims to empower communities through data governance, it operates primarily through academic research and institutional partnerships rather than providing direct open tools to practitioners, with unclear practical benefits to end users.

Open source decentralized documentation platform scores moderately on free access (60/100) and anti-extraction (50/100), but lacks evidence of direct practitioner benefits versus institutional efficiency (20/100).

The Decelerator provides free support to civil society organizations facing endings, scoring moderately on practitioner benefit and anti-extraction principles, but lacking open source architecture and serving organizations rather than individual practitioners.

Strong open-source participatory democracy platform with genuine free access and anti-extraction design, but primarily serves institutional actors (governments) rather than direct practitioners, limiting its score on criterion 2.

While the platform promotes reuse and efficiency in government digital services, it primarily serves institutional actors (government departments) rather than individual practitioners or communities, lacks evidence of removing access barriers for underserved groups, and operates within government infrastructure rather than promoting independence from institutional platforms.

While the project provides free access to parliamentary data (partial credit on criterion 1), it primarily serves institutional transparency rather than empowering individual practitioners, and appears to be a government-operated service rather than an independent tool challenging extraction.

Strong alignment on open access (open-source, free API) and direct practitioner benefit (serves voters and civic developers), but moderate extraction stance due to Electoral Services Council partnerships.

A government-funded technical standard that serves institutional actors and technology developers rather than practitioners, lacks open access (not open source), and operates within existing corporate/government infrastructure rather than providing independence from it.

Free resource serving nonprofits meets access criteria but lacks open source status, serves organizations rather than individual practitioners, and shows no evidence of platform independence architecture.

Pear scores well on open access (MIT licensed, free) and anti-extraction (peer-to-peer architecture bypassing corporate platforms), but lacks clear evidence of direct practitioner benefits beyond developer tooling.

Open-source collaborative tool scores well on free access (MIT license, no pricing) but serves organizations rather than individual practitioners, and lacks evidence of anti-extraction design or platform independence.

Closed-source freemium platform with tiered pricing model directly contradicts criterion 1 (free/open access), while serving grassroots activists meets criterion 2 but insufficient evidence on platform independence for criterion 3.

While Dovetail serves non-profits, it functions as a closed platform connecting organizations to service providers rather than providing free tools directly to practitioners, with no evidence of open source code or anti-extraction design principles.
Proprietary platform serving organizations rather than individual practitioners, with no open source components and limited transparency, contradicting all three core criteria.

Strong alignment on open access (framework is open source) and direct benefit to civil society practitioners and marginalized communities in AI governance, but loses points on anti-extraction criterion as it works within existing corporate AI platforms rather than building alternatives to them.

Wikipedia's In the News scores well on open access (fully free, open-source) and anti-extraction (no corporate ownership, volunteer-driven), but serves primarily as institutional infrastructure rather than directly empowering individual practitioners or marginalized communities.

Scores moderately well on free access (no paywall) and direct practitioner benefit (helps individuals claim benefits), but loses points for government dependency and lack of open source infrastructure.

Proprietary platform serving government agencies with subscription model contradicts all three core criteria: closed-source (criterion 1), benefits institutions over practitioners (criterion 2), and creates vendor lock-in dependencies (criterion 3).

While Ethelo serves some community engagement purposes, it operates as a proprietary SaaS platform with subscription-based access that primarily benefits institutional clients rather than individual practitioners, contradicting all three core criteria of open access, direct practitioner benefit, and platform independence.

While Diia demonstrates genuine open-source commitment and serves individual citizens directly, it fundamentally strengthens government institutional power rather than empowering practitioners against intermediaries, and creates new state-controlled digital infrastructure dependencies.
Platform cooperative model directly benefits hosts and communities over corporate intermediaries, though partial open-source status and subscription model limit full accessibility.

While serving smallholder farmers aligns with practitioner focus, the closed-source nature, dependency on corporate funders like Gates Foundation, and centralized governance by Digital Green contradict core criteria of open access and platform independence.

While partially open-source and free to use, Fatebook primarily serves researchers and decision-makers rather than marginalized practitioners, and its reliance on Open Philanthropy funding suggests insufficient independence from institutional actors.

While serving journalists and researchers, Filmot is closed-source, relies on YouTube's corporate infrastructure rather than providing independence from it, and primarily benefits already-resourced practitioners rather than removing access barriers.

Strong on serving practitioners (social housing tenants) with free access, but loses points for closed-source architecture and dependency on institutional partnerships rather than platform independence.

Proprietary SaaS platform serving well-resourced fact-checking organizations through paid licenses, with no open source components and dependency on corporate platforms, contradicting all three core criteria.
Government-operated transparency platform that serves institutional compliance needs more than individual practitioners, with closed-source architecture and no community ownership model.

ODK scores well on open access (fully open-source, MIT licensed) and anti-extraction (no corporate platform dependencies), but loses points for primarily serving institutional actors (NGOs, government agencies) rather than direct practitioners, with funding from major institutional donors like Gates Foundation and USAID.

Open-source tool serving individual journalists and researchers with free access to corporate accountability data, though it operates within existing SEC infrastructure rather than creating alternatives to it.

Open-source AT Protocol implementation prioritizing community safety scores well on free access and anti-extraction, but primary beneficiaries appear to be platform users generally rather than specific practitioners or marginalized communities.

While open source and attempting decentralization, Bluesky's venture capital funding model and platform architecture primarily benefit the company rather than individual practitioners, failing to meet Frederick's anti-extraction and direct-benefit criteria.

Strong alignment with all three criteria: fully open-source tool (MIT license implied by GitHub), directly benefits individual internet users by automating privacy choices, and explicitly bypasses corporate surveillance infrastructure by enforcing user consent preferences against tracking platforms.

Polis scores moderately well on open access (fully open-source, MIT licensed) but loses significant points for primarily serving governments and institutions rather than individual practitioners, and for lacking evidence of platform independence or anti-extraction design principles.

PatCit scores moderately well as an open-source dataset (MIT licensed) serving researchers and policy analysts, though it depends on Google BigQuery infrastructure and appears to have stalled development since 2020.

While open source (MIT licensed) and serving health workers, the project primarily benefits institutional actors (ministries, NGOs) rather than individual practitioners, and lacks evidence of platform independence or anti-extraction design.

While the project offers partial open-source access to a powerful AI model, it primarily serves well-resourced researchers and developers rather than marginalized communities, is VC-funded by major firms, and operates within corporate AI infrastructure rather than providing independence from it.

While open source and CC-BY-4.0 licensed, the framework primarily serves institutional actors (NATO, EU, government units) rather than individual practitioners, and includes concerning authoritarian TTPs that could enable state surveillance infrastructure.

While open source (MIT licensed), this Web3 infrastructure project primarily serves blockchain developers rather than end-user communities, lacks evidence of removing access barriers for marginalized groups, and operates within corporate blockchain ecosystems rather than providing platform independence.

Open-source civic consultation platform scores well on access (MIT license, free) but serves government-citizen intermediation rather than direct practitioner empowerment, with strong government partnerships potentially limiting independence.

PlaceCal scores well on open access (MIT licensed, free platform) and community benefit (serves local organizers and citizens directly), but lacks clear evidence of anti-extraction design or platform independence in the dossier.

HURIDOCS scores well on open access (open source tools, GitHub presence) and direct practitioner benefit (serving human rights defenders and civil society), but loses points for organizational funding model and institutional partnerships that don't fully align with anti-extraction stance.

While open source and freely accessible, this government-maintained dataset catalog primarily serves institutional actors (government departments, researchers) rather than individual practitioners, and strengthens government data infrastructure without challenging extractive intermediaries.

Open-source API democratizing UK postcode data access scores well on free access (15/20) and practitioner benefit (13/20), but corporate ownership and freemium model limit anti-extraction score (7/20).
Open-source, zero-login calendar tool serving grassroots organizers scores well on access and practitioner benefit, but lacks evidence of anti-extraction design and has Firebase dependency.

Mastodon scores well on open access (fully open source, self-hostable) and anti-extraction (explicitly bypasses corporate platforms), but serves a mix of individual practitioners and institutional actors rather than focusing exclusively on marginalized communities.

Open source MIT-licensed project (criterion 1: 80%) serving individual policy researchers rather than institutions (criterion 2: 60%), but lacks evidence of platform independence and relies on proprietary AI models (criterion 3: 20%), with experimental framework showing no documented policy impact or democratic input mechanisms.
Open-source research tool for DAO governance analysis scores moderately on free access and practitioner benefit, but lacks evidence of anti-extraction design or direct community impact.

Open source collaborative democracy tool serving individual citizens and activists with genuine free access, though GitHub dependency and limited adoption beyond original use case temper the anti-extraction and practitioner benefit scores.

Open source party participation platform scores well on access and practitioner benefit but loses points for platform dependencies and serving primarily party infrastructure rather than independent civic action.

Open-source civic engagement tools score moderately: strong on access (open-source, free) but primarily serve government institutions rather than bypassing them, with no evidence of anti-extraction design.
Open source tool (MIT license presumed) serving journalists directly scores well on access and practitioner benefit, but lacks evidence of platform independence and appears dormant since 2019.
Open-source governance platform serving citizens directly scores well on access and practitioner benefit, but lacks evidence of anti-extraction design and shows dependency on pol.is infrastructure.
Open-source citizen petition platform serving individuals over institutions, though limited evidence on corporate independence and some institutional partnerships implied.

Open-source tool enabling journalists and researchers to investigate corporate networks through UK Companies House data, though limited by solo development and lack of documented community engagement.

Open-source tool (MIT license) serving researchers rather than institutions scores well on access, but lacks evidence of removing meaningful barriers or benefiting practitioners over platforms, and depends heavily on corporate AI APIs.

Open-source participatory budgeting platform scores moderately well on free access (MIT license, GitHub hosted) and direct community benefit, but loses points for serving government institutions rather than bypassing them and for lacking evidence of anti-extraction design principles.

Open source tool that democratizes access to election campaign data for researchers and journalists, though reliance on proprietary GPT-4 Vision API and serving already-resourced analysts limits alignment with practitioner-first and anti-extraction principles.

Open-source transparency tool serving researchers and journalists to analyze platform misinformation systems, though limited by dependency on X/Twitter's continued data availability and single-maintainer structure.

Scores moderately on open access (MIT licensed, free) but low on practitioner benefit (enables automation that may violate terms of service) and anti-extraction stance (depends entirely on WhatsApp's proprietary infrastructure).

Open source framework (criterion 1) serving developers rather than end-user practitioners (criterion 2), with unclear platform independence given Ethereum dependency and association with 2016 DAO hack raising extraction concerns (criterion 3).

Strong on open access (MIT licensed, GitHub hosted) and anti-extraction (creates standards for platform transparency), moderate on practitioner benefit (serves journalists/researchers but also platforms themselves), with positive modifiers for international scope and policy influence.

youtube-dl exemplifies O'Brien's values through free open-source access (MIT-style), direct benefit to journalists/archivists bypassing platform restrictions, and anti-extraction design that liberates content from corporate platform control.

While serving fact-checkers and citizens, the project is closed-source, institutionally dependent on IFCN/EFCSN, and appears to strengthen existing fact-checking organizations rather than empowering independent practitioners or removing access barriers.

Open-source educational tool for policy makers scores well on access (GitHub, MIT license implied) but serves institutional actors rather than practitioners, with no evidence of anti-extraction design principles.

Government platform that centralizes consultation access but remains closed-source, institutionally-controlled, and reinforces existing power structures rather than empowering practitioners or communities directly.

Proprietary government platform serving institutional clients rather than practitioners, with subscription-based access model and Vista Equity Partners ownership structure that contradicts all three core criteria.

Proprietary B2B SaaS platform serving government agencies contradicts all three core criteria: closed-source (not open access), primarily benefits institutions over practitioners, and operates within rather than against corporate/surveillance infrastructure.

GrantNav scores moderately as a transparency platform that makes UK grant data searchable and downloadable, but serves institutional funders as much as communities and relies on voluntary data sharing rather than challenging extractive systems.

GreenPT fails all three criteria: it's a closed-source commercial platform (not open access), serves governments and businesses rather than individual practitioners, and despite privacy claims, remains dependent on proprietary models and centralized infrastructure rather than offering true platform independence.

Guardian Project exemplifies Frederick's values through genuinely open-source privacy tools that directly serve journalists and activists at risk, explicitly bypassing corporate surveillance infrastructure while maintaining complete independence from platform control.

While the standards are partially open source and serve social housing providers, they primarily benefit institutional actors (housing associations) rather than individual practitioners or residents, and don't challenge extractive platform dynamics.

A potentially valuable tool for digitizing grassroots petitions that appears to be open source and serves activists directly, but the dead link and lack of concrete implementation details prevent higher scoring on all three criteria.

Proprietary AI platform serving organizations through paid subscriptions contradicts all three core criteria: closed-source with access barriers, benefits institutions over practitioners, and depends on corporate AI infrastructure.
Free workshops removing barriers to data science education for underrepresented groups align with open access and practitioner benefit criteria, though platform independence is unclear.

While Idealist provides valuable civic infrastructure, it operates as a for-profit platform with subscription models that gate access to core functionality, serves primarily well-resourced nonprofits rather than individual practitioners, and maintains a centralized corporate structure rather than enabling platform independence.

JOSS exemplifies all three criteria by providing free, open-source publishing infrastructure that directly benefits individual researchers and developers while explicitly rejecting extractive APC/subscription models that dominate academic publishing.

While providing free tools to journalists, this Google-owned platform deepens dependence on corporate surveillance infrastructure rather than enabling independence from it, directly contradicting Frederick's core anti-extraction principle.
Kialo's proprietary platform with subscription model and platform-managed governance contradicts all three core criteria despite serving educators and students.

While Labour Xchange serves underemployed workers and marginalized communities, it operates as a closed-source, subscription-based platform that maintains rather than disrupts traditional employment intermediation structures.

While serving low-income workers aligns with practitioner focus, the closed-source platform model with major corporate funders (Google.org) and lack of transparency contradicts Frederick's core values of open access and platform independence.

While Land Explorer serves community organizations directly and addresses land access barriers, it is not open source, partners with government institutions rather than bypassing them, and lacks evidence of challenging extractive platforms or surveillance infrastructure.

Libertrium is a closed-source, for-profit platform serving government institutions rather than individual practitioners, with subscription-based revenue model and no evidence of removing access barriers for communities.

Strong on open access (MIT licensed, multilingual) and practitioner benefit (serves civil society/activists), but funded by major foundations and lacks evidence of platform independence or anti-extraction design.

Strong open-source credentials and direct practitioner benefit through liquid democracy tools, but dual commercial model and documented power concentration risks in delegation chains prevent higher scoring.

LittleSis exemplifies Frederick's values through its free, open-source power-mapping database that directly serves journalists, activists, and researchers rather than institutions, while operating independently of corporate platforms to expose elite networks.

Dead link (404) with minimal verifiable information prevents assessment of open access, practitioner benefits, or platform independence - conservative low score reflects lack of evidence rather than negative assessment.
Subscription-based data platform serving institutional actors (councils, grantmakers) rather than individual practitioners, with no open source components and dependency on continued funding access.

Open-source decentralized infrastructure serving individual practitioners scores well on access and anti-extraction, but early testnet status and lack of documented impact limit assessment of actual community benefit.

A VC-funded prediction market platform that, while partially open source, operates as a for-profit intermediary extracting value from user-generated markets rather than directly empowering practitioners or communities.

MapIt scores moderately as a partially open-source civic infrastructure tool that primarily serves government agencies and developers rather than directly empowering individual practitioners, while its subscription model and reliance on UK government data partnerships limit its independence from institutional frameworks.

Scores well on free access (partial open source, no pricing mentioned) and practitioner benefit (serves grassroots organisers/activists), but lacks evidence of anti-extraction design or platform independence.
Educational mapping platform scores moderately on practitioner benefit but lacks evidence of open source status, anti-extraction design, or removal of access barriers.

Matrix scores highly as a genuinely open protocol (Apache 2.0 licensed) that directly empowers individuals and communities to communicate without platform intermediaries, though government partnerships and Element's central role in development present some tension with pure anti-extraction principles.

Dead link and minimal evidence prevent proper assessment, but open-source status and decentralized governance focus earn modest points on criteria 1 and 3, while lack of deployment details limits practitioner benefit scoring.
Open-source governance tool scores moderately on access (GitHub confirmed) but lacks evidence of direct practitioner benefit or platform independence, with dead link preventing deeper assessment.

A parliamentary transparency database scores moderately on free access (appears to have been public) and practitioner benefit (serving journalists/researchers), but loses points for being government-operated rather than independent, and is currently offline.

Abstract Wikipedia scores well on free/open access (open source, no paywalls) and anti-extraction (nonprofit Wikimedia infrastructure), but serves institutions/platforms more than individual practitioners despite its multilingual knowledge democratization goals.

While Metaculus provides some open access to forecasting tools, it operates as a for-profit platform with subscription tiers, serves primarily researchers and policymakers rather than marginalized practitioners, and depends on corporate grant funding rather than maintaining independence from institutional actors.
Partially open-source academic platform serving researchers and governance practitioners lacks evidence of removing access barriers or directly benefiting individual practitioners over institutions.
Strong on practitioner benefit and anti-extraction stance through civic data transparency work, but loses points on open access due to campaign/publication format rather than open tools.

While the project provides free public access to political accountability data, it primarily serves as a monitoring dashboard rather than empowering practitioners directly, and its reliance on corporate prediction markets (Polymarket, Kalshi) contradicts the anti-extraction stance.

While the platform provides free access to ethical deliberation tools, it primarily serves academic researchers and AI developers rather than empowering individual practitioners, and its institutional dependency on MIT Media Lab contradicts the anti-extraction stance.

Open protocol for decentralized cooperative mapping scores well on free access and anti-extraction principles, moderately on practitioner benefit, but lacks clear evidence of direct economic routing to individuals versus organizations.

While serving civil society groups addressing disinformation, the project is closed-source, institutionally controlled by Oxford, and operates as a curated resource rather than providing direct tools to practitioners.

A proprietary, subscription-based platform serving organizations rather than individual practitioners, with no open-source components and dependency on centralized infrastructure — directly contradicting all three core criteria.

While Roundabout serves local communities directly and avoids algorithmic virality, it scores poorly on open access (closed source, limited beta), lacks clear platform independence architecture, and shows insufficient evidence of addressing structural inequalities beyond general community building.
Closed-source platform serving organizations rather than individual practitioners, with public funding but no evidence of removing access barriers or platform independence.

While NumFOCUS champions open source scientific tools, its primary beneficiaries are institutions and researchers rather than marginalized practitioners, and it relies heavily on corporate sponsorships from tech giants rather than maintaining platform independence.

Strong on free access (no paywalls, partial open-source) and direct community benefit (serves marginalized groups with legal literacy), but dependent on institutional backing (Vidhi Centre) and philanthropic funding rather than fully community-owned.

While Nym provides open-source privacy infrastructure that serves individual users against surveillance, its VC funding model, commercial VPN service with pricing tiers, and lack of explicit focus on marginalized communities or practitioners limit its alignment with Frederick's values.

While OA.Report promotes research transparency, it is a closed-source subscription platform primarily serving well-resourced institutional funders rather than individual practitioners, contradicting all three core criteria.

OA.Works exemplifies Frederick's values through genuinely open-source tools that bypass publisher paywalls to directly serve researchers and librarians globally, though some dependency on institutional funding tempers the anti-extraction stance.

Scores moderately on practitioner benefit (15/20) and anti-extraction (10/20) by empowering individual citizens against planning decisions, but fails on open access (0/20) due to subscription model and closed-source nature.

Strong alignment on free/open access (MIT license, no-code tool for non-programmers) and direct practitioner benefit (serves data journalists, activists, nonprofits), but moderate on anti-extraction due to institutional dependencies and no explicit platform resistance features.

Scores moderately well on open access (open source, free platform) and community benefit (funding underrepresented groups), but loses points for dependency on philanthropic capital and platform not yet publicly launched at scale.
Open-source tool serving individual bike theft victims scores well on access and anti-extraction, but limited impact on practitioners and unclear adoption pathway temper the overall assessment.
A transparency database serving journalists and researchers aligns with practitioner-focused values, but the dead link status and unclear access model prevent higher scoring on open access criteria.

A proprietary commercial SaaS platform that serves political organizations and campaigners but fails all three core criteria: it's not open source, primarily benefits organizations rather than individual practitioners, and operates as a centralized commercial platform rather than promoting independence from corporate infrastructure.

While OpenBudgets.eu provides partial open access to budget visualization tools, it primarily serves government agencies and institutional actors rather than individual practitioners, and its EU funding model suggests institutional rather than community-driven independence.

Open Collective scores well on free access (open source, no barriers) and direct practitioner benefit (serves grassroots groups, not institutions), but loses points on platform dependence as it operates as a centralized platform rather than enabling full independence.

Strong alignment on free access (open source, no paywalls) and direct community benefit (citizens over institutions), but moderate on anti-extraction due to reliance on council cooperation and conventional web infrastructure rather than decentralized alternatives.
A proprietary, subscription-based database that serves well-resourced campaigners and organizations rather than removing barriers for individual practitioners or communities.

Government-operated platform with partial open access scores poorly on practitioner benefit and platform independence criteria, further penalized for announced discontinuation affecting researchers and communities.

Open-source planning tools serving local government practitioners score moderately on access and anti-extraction, but primarily benefit institutional actors rather than individual practitioners or communities.

Strong alignment on open access (MIT licensed, donation-based) and community benefit (gift-based gatherings, peer evaluation), but limited evidence of platform independence and early-stage status prevents higher scoring.
Platform model serving advocacy groups lacks open source commitment, creates intermediary layer between citizens and institutions, and shows no evidence of anti-extraction design principles.

Strong alignment on open access (MIT licensed, free API) and direct practitioner benefit (serves citizens/journalists not government), but limited evidence of anti-extraction stance beyond being independent of government platforms.

While open source and transparency-focused, OpenProcurement primarily serves government institutions and procurement agencies rather than individual practitioners, with benefits flowing through institutional efficiency rather than direct empowerment of communities or removal of access barriers for marginalized groups.

While genuinely open source and standardizing community services data access, the project primarily serves government institutions rather than directly empowering practitioners or communities, and operates within rather than challenging existing institutional frameworks.

Open source platform serving workers and advocacy groups scores well on access and anti-extraction, but corporate partnerships and multi-stakeholder governance model limit practitioner-first benefits.

While ORCID provides free researcher identifiers and has partial open-source components, it primarily serves institutional needs through subscription models and lacks the practitioner-first, anti-extraction design principles prioritized in this constitution.

OSF exemplifies Frederick's values through free, open-source research infrastructure that directly empowers individual researchers rather than institutions, while maintaining independence from corporate platforms through community governance.

Strong alignment on open access (GitHub, free tools) and practitioner benefit (journalists, researchers), but insufficient evidence on anti-extraction stance and potential dual-use concerns for surveillance applications.

Overton is a proprietary, subscription-based platform serving well-resourced institutions (universities, governments, think tanks) rather than individual practitioners, with no open-source components and a business model that reinforces rather than challenges existing power structures in policy research.

While the project promotes participatory principles in AI procurement, it primarily serves institutional actors (government procurement officials, policymakers) rather than direct practitioners, and lacks evidence of removing access barriers or platform independence.

Strong alignment on free/open access (MIT licensed, no fees) and direct practitioner benefit (serves journalists/researchers not institutions), but lacks explicit anti-extraction stance and depends on Wikimedia infrastructure.
Dead link to unknown academic paper with minimal dossier information prevents assessment of open access, practitioner benefit, or platform independence criteria.

Scores moderately on practitioner benefit (serves citizens/journalists) and anti-extraction (nonprofit model), but lacks evidence of open source access and appears to work within existing institutional frameworks rather than bypassing them.

While the project provides free access to parliamentary bill summaries for citizens and advocacy groups, it relies on unverified AI-generated content without open-sourcing its tools, creating potential misinformation risks without transparency or accountability mechanisms.

Parti scores moderately as a government-partnered platform that, while enabling citizen participation, primarily serves municipal institutions rather than empowering practitioners directly, with partial open-source status and dependency on government funding limiting its independence from institutional infrastructure.

While Participedia provides free, open-source access to democratic innovation knowledge (scoring well on Criterion 1), it primarily serves academic researchers and institutions rather than direct practitioners, and relies heavily on academic grant funding rather than achieving platform independence.

Closed-source platform serving primarily local authorities and developers through subscription model, with dead website suggesting project failure, contradicts all three core criteria of open access, practitioner benefit, and platform independence.
Strong on open access (partial open source, free tier) and anti-extraction (privacy-first alternative to Google Analytics), but serves primarily website owners rather than marginalized practitioners.
Community-focused platform scores moderately on serving practitioners over institutions, but lacks evidence of open access (closed source) and anti-extraction design principles.

Strong alignment on all three criteria: genuinely open-source tax/benefit modeling tools (MIT license, GitHub presence), directly serves practitioners and citizens rather than institutions, and operates independently of corporate platforms while being used by diverse stakeholders from think tanks to advocacy groups.

Open-source governance tool for online communities scores moderately well on access (MIT license, GitHub) and practitioner benefit, but loses points for academic institutional backing and reliance on corporate platform APIs.

A subscription-based proprietary platform serving public affairs professionals fails all three criteria: it's not open access, it primarily benefits organizations rather than individual practitioners, and it operates as a centralized corporate platform.

PostBug fails all three criteria: it's a subscription-based service (not free/open), serves advocacy organizations rather than individual practitioners, and operates through a parent company (FairSay) rather than providing platform independence.

Privacy Badger exemplifies Frederick's values: free open-source tool (MIT license), directly empowers individual users against corporate surveillance infrastructure, and explicitly bypasses platform tracking mechanisms while serving practitioners like journalists and activists.

Closed-source educational tool serving general public through a nonprofit model scores poorly on all three criteria: not open access (proprietary), serves individuals but through an institutional platform rather than directly empowering practitioners, and depends on centralized web infrastructure rather than promoting independence.

While providing civic data access serves practitioners and communities, the project relies on proprietary Tableau infrastructure, lacks open source components, and primarily benefits an established charity rather than removing institutional barriers.

A public records database serving journalists and researchers scores moderately well on practitioner benefit and anti-extraction principles, but loses significant points for being closed-source with no evidence of free access model.

Public AI scores well on open access (open-source, free API) and anti-extraction (sovereign models, public compute), but serves primarily institutions and developers rather than individual practitioners.

A curated database of media tools that serves organizations rather than individual practitioners, lacks open source commitment, and appears to catalog rather than challenge existing platform dependencies.
Open-source collaboration tool for activists and journalists scores well on free access and practitioner benefit, but limited evidence on platform independence and economic sustainability model.

Open-source voting tool serving practitioners and communities scores well on access and anti-extraction, but moderate on direct benefit due to organizational focus and limited evidence of displacing extractive intermediaries.

Strong alignment on all three criteria: fully open-source peer-to-peer forge that removes GitHub dependency, directly serves individual developers rather than organizations, and explicitly bypasses corporate platform control through decentralized architecture.

Open-source neighborhood tools serving grassroots organizers align with practitioner-first values, though limited dossier evidence prevents full assessment of anti-extraction stance and platform independence.
Free SMS voter reminder service scores moderately by serving individual voters directly and removing cost barriers, but lacks open source commitment and depends on centralized SMS infrastructure.

A government-operated research repository that serves institutional actors rather than practitioners, lacks open source implementation, and strengthens existing government infrastructure without removing barriers for communities.
Open-source tool directly serving unions and civic groups scores well on access and practitioner benefit, but abandoned prototype status and platform dependencies significantly limit impact.

Scores well on serving practitioners/communities (environmental justice advocates) and anti-extraction stance (nonprofit model), but loses significant points for not being open source despite being a digital toolkit.

Riseup exemplifies Frederick's values through free secure communication tools for activists, direct practitioner benefit bypassing corporate surveillance infrastructure, and 25+ years of volunteer-driven service despite government pressure.

While the project provides free access to environmental data visualization, it primarily serves institutional researchers and policymakers rather than individual practitioners, and relies heavily on corporate platform infrastructure (Twitter/X API) for its core functionality.

While Schema.org is open source and community-governed, it primarily serves large tech corporations (Google, Microsoft, Yahoo, Yandex) to standardize web data structures rather than directly empowering individual practitioners or removing access barriers.

Sci-Hub exemplifies all three core criteria by providing free access to paywalled academic research (criterion 1), directly benefiting individual researchers and students rather than institutions (criterion 2), and operating independently of corporate publishing platforms through decentralized infrastructure (criterion 3).

Open source security tools directly serving journalists and activists in high-risk environments, bypassing institutional gatekeepers while maintaining platform independence through FOSS licensing and decentralized distribution.

SecureDrop exemplifies Frederick's values through open-source architecture that directly empowers individual journalists and whistleblowers while bypassing surveillance infrastructure, though it requires institutional hosting which slightly limits pure practitioner autonomy.

Open-source climate science database serving researchers and journalists scores well on access (MIT license, no paywalls) and practitioner benefit, but lacks evidence of platform independence infrastructure and has minimal documentation about actual implementation.

Strong alignment across all criteria: removes paywalls to academic knowledge (C1), directly serves individual researchers bypassing publisher gatekeeping (C2), and provides infrastructure independent of commercial academic publishers (C3).

Proprietary AI platform serving government clients with subscription model and no open source components contradicts all three core criteria of free access, practitioner benefit, and platform independence.

Strong alignment on free/open access (MIT licensed, cooperative model) and direct practitioner benefit (funds FOSS developers directly), but limited evidence of anti-extraction stance beyond cooperative structure, and still in alpha with small user base limits impact assessment.

A proprietary, subscription-based platform serving organizations and government agencies rather than individual practitioners, with no open-source components and dependency on corporate messaging platforms.

While the project champions ethical technology values and serves individual practitioners over institutions, it lacks concrete open-source tools, clear governance structures, and demonstrated independence from corporate platforms.

Strong alignment across all criteria: open-source platform removing access barriers to critical documents (Criterion 1), directly serving investigative journalists and civil society rather than institutions (Criterion 2), and operating independently from corporate platforms while enabling pan-African collaboration (Criterion 3).

Open-source tool serving individual data practitioners scores well on access and anti-extraction, but limited activity since 2021 and privacy concerns around automated identity linking constrain the score.

Open-source Matrix-based tool enabling decentralized group-to-group communication directly benefits communities while bypassing corporate platforms, though limited dossier evidence prevents full assessment of access barriers and practitioner focus.

Proprietary platform for collective action that fails all three criteria: closed-source with no open access model, serves organizations more than individual practitioners, and creates platform dependency rather than independence.

While the guidebook is open source and freely accessible, it primarily serves institutional actors (ODI, government partners) in creating data standards rather than directly empowering individual practitioners or communities against extractive platforms.

Strike Map exemplifies Frederick's values through free access to labor organizing data, direct benefit to workers and organizers rather than institutions, and independence from corporate platforms while building grassroots infrastructure.

Partial open-source status and reliance on AI/LLM infrastructure contradict anti-extraction principles, while government partnerships and institutional focus dilute practitioner-first benefits, though the tool does serve some community groups directly.

A grassroots, open-source directory that directly serves technology workers seeking cooperative alternatives to corporate employment structures, though impact is limited to information provision rather than direct tool creation.

While The List directly serves individual fundraisers and nonprofits rather than institutions, it lacks open source access, depends on a single maintainer, and operates without transparent governance or verification processes that would ensure procedural legitimacy.

Strong alignment on free access (open data platform) and direct community benefit (serves defendants, journalists, public defenders), but partial dependence on institutional partners and frozen 2018 dataset limit anti-extraction score.

Strong on open access (MIT licensed, free API) and practitioner benefit (serves journalists/researchers directly), but limited anti-extraction stance as it depends on government infrastructure rather than building alternatives.
A report on data governance that serves institutional actors rather than practitioners, lacks open access implementation, and operates within existing power structures without challenging extraction.

While Timecounts serves community organizations, it fails all three core criteria: it's a proprietary subscription-based platform (not open access), primarily benefits organizations rather than individual practitioners, and creates ongoing platform dependency rather than independence.
Minimal dossier with no evidence of open source status, unclear beneficiaries beyond 'general public', and no information about platform independence or anti-extraction design.

Mixed performance: serves practitioners directly and provides transparency tools, but operates behind paywalls/subscriptions and depends entirely on corporate platform APIs rather than building independent infrastructure.
Free tool serving grassroots organizers scores well on access and practitioner benefit, but dependency on Google infrastructure contradicts anti-extraction criterion.
Worker-led platform that directly empowers gig workers against corporate extraction, providing free open-source tools for mutual aid and collective bargaining on Amazon's Mechanical Turk platform.

Strong alignment across all criteria: genuinely open source tool that removes paywalls to academic knowledge, directly benefits individual researchers/students/journalists rather than institutions, and operates independently of corporate publishing platforms while actively circumventing their extraction model.

Strong on open access (open source, free, multilingual) but serves institutional actors alongside individuals and depends on foundation funding rather than achieving full independence from corporate/institutional structures.

While Urbit promotes digital sovereignty and independence from corporate platforms, its high technical barriers, VC funding model, and corporate control by Tlon Corporation limit its accessibility and community ownership, failing to fully embody Frederick's values of removing access barriers and serving practitioners directly.

While VFRAME provides valuable tools for human rights documentation, it primarily serves well-resourced NGOs and institutions rather than individual practitioners, lacks full open-source commitment, and depends on EU funding and partnerships rather than maintaining platform independence.
Closed-source, VC-funded platform that serves organizations rather than individual practitioners, with opaque AI systems and no evidence of removing access barriers to democratic participation tools.

Project shows mixed alignment: serves individual practitioners (journalists, researchers) but is not open source, has limited access due to technical barriers, and appears to be institutionally controlled rather than community-owned.

While the project provides free access to policy comparison tools for individual voters, it lacks open source code, serves institutional parties as much as citizens, and operates within rather than against existing platform structures.

While WardWatch serves individual citizens and voters with free access to council performance data, its proprietary nature, subscription funding model, and lack of open source code significantly limit its alignment with Frederick's core values of open access and platform independence.

The Internet Archive exemplifies free and open access to knowledge preservation, directly serves practitioners like journalists and researchers rather than institutions, and operates independently from corporate platforms while maintaining transparency through open-source tools and public benefit mission.

A proprietary, subscription-based platform serving primarily corporate and institutional actors (cybersecurity teams, legal professionals, corporate intelligence) rather than individual practitioners or marginalized communities, with no open-source components and a business model that reinforces rather than challenges existing power structures.
Tool provides free access to researchers but fundamentally depends on and legitimizes Facebook's surveillance infrastructure rather than offering independence from it.

While this community network supports tech-for-good practitioners, it operates on a proprietary platform (Slack), lacks open-source tools, and primarily serves already-resourced agencies and consultancies rather than removing barriers for marginalized practitioners.

While Campaign Tracker provides free access to political transparency data serving journalists and citizens, it operates through institutional partnerships and funding rather than empowering individual practitioners to bypass gatekeepers.

Community Tech Network scores moderately well for serving community organizations and local communities directly, but lacks evidence of open source tools and appears to function primarily as an information resource rather than providing free access to actual technology tools.

Project lacks substantive information to assess open access, practitioner benefits, or platform independence, with vague claims about 'civilizational singularity' and no evidence of actual tools or implementation.

While CrowdJustice democratizes access to legal funding for individuals, it operates as a VC-funded for-profit platform that takes fees from campaigns rather than providing truly free and open access to justice tools.

Partial open source tool for collective summarization scores moderately on free access (partial open source, no pricing info) and practitioner benefit (serves discussion participants directly), but lacks evidence of anti-extraction design or platform independence.

A proprietary B2B SaaS platform serving governments and organizations rather than individual practitioners, with closed-source code, corporate control, and dependency on third-party infrastructure — directly contradicting all three core criteria of open access, practitioner benefit, and platform independence.
Closed-source network serving primarily technologists and experts rather than end practitioners, with invite-only membership and no evidence of removing access barriers or platform independence.

Open source civic tech tools score moderately on free access (criterion 1) but serve institutional actors like election officials alongside individual voters, and maintain government partnerships rather than platform independence.

While Discourse is open-source and enables community participation, it primarily serves well-resourced organizations through a VC-backed subscription model rather than removing barriers for individual practitioners or marginalized communities.

DoNotPay fails all three core criteria: it's a proprietary, VC-funded subscription platform (not open access), serves individual consumers but through a centralized corporate intermediary rather than empowering practitioners directly, and represents platform dependence rather than independence from corporate infrastructure.

A subscription-based publication serving established nonprofits with grant-making data scores low on all criteria: not open access, serves organizations rather than individual practitioners, and operates within traditional institutional fundraising infrastructure.

While FixMyStreet provides free civic reporting tools with partial open source code, it primarily serves as an efficiency layer for existing government institutions rather than empowering individual practitioners or communities to bypass institutional gatekeeping.

While GOV.UK Forms provides free access to government form creation tools, it primarily serves government departments rather than individual practitioners, and operates within rather than challenging existing institutional structures.

Give Food scores well on free access (open data platform, partial open source) and direct community benefit (serves food banks and citizens), but lacks evidence of platform independence and appears to work within existing institutional frameworks rather than bypassing them.

GlobaLeaks scores highly across all criteria: genuinely free and open-source (MIT license, GitHub), directly serves whistleblowers and journalists rather than institutions, and explicitly enables platform-independent secure communications infrastructure.

While the Service Manual is open access and promotes good digital service design, it primarily serves government institutions rather than individual practitioners, is operated by government rather than independent of corporate/state platforms, and focuses on institutional efficiency over direct community empowerment.
A proprietary SaaS platform serving government institutions through subscription models, with closed-source AI analysis and no evidence of direct practitioner benefit or platform independence.

Strong on free access (no paywalls, partial open source) and direct practitioner benefit (serves journalists, researchers, citizens), but maintains dependencies on government data feeds and institutional partnerships rather than full platform independence.

Proprietary AI platform serving businesses and government procurement teams with subscription-based access violates all three core criteria: closed-source with paywalls, benefits organizations over practitioners, and creates platform dependency rather than independence.

HOT scores well on free access (OpenStreetMap-based, partial open source) and direct community benefit (serves affected communities and local mappers), but corporate funding dependencies (Google, Microsoft, Mapbox) and institutional focus (UN, World Bank partnerships) limit its anti-extraction stance.

Platform serves climate campaigners directly but is closed-source with members-only data restrictions, operated by established NGOs rather than being community-owned, and depends on institutional partnerships rather than providing independent infrastructure.

Loomio scores moderately well as an open-source decision-making platform serving practitioners and communities directly, though its subscription model and LLC structure limit its anti-extraction stance.

Platform serves individual renters against institutional landlords (criterion 2: high) but is closed-source with no open access model documented (criterion 1: low) and partners with government/universities rather than maintaining independence (criterion 3: medium).
Strong alignment on free/open access and direct practitioner benefit for human rights defenders, but discontinued maintenance since 2018 creates serious security vulnerabilities for at-risk users.

While partially open-source with some public benefit claims, this for-profit consultancy primarily serves government agencies and institutions rather than individual practitioners, with dependency on government contracts and limited transparency on proprietary methods.

Strong alignment across all criteria: open-source cooperative platform providing surveillance-free video conferencing that directly serves activists and educators while explicitly bypassing corporate tech infrastructure.

Strong on free access (open-source, GitHub available) and practitioner benefit (serves journalists/researchers directly), but lacks anti-extraction stance as it analyzes Twitter/X data without challenging platform dependency.

MP Watch scores moderately as it provides free access to accountability tools for citizens but operates through traditional advocacy channels rather than disintermediating institutional power, with insufficient evidence of open-source commitment or platform independence.

A closed-source, NationBuilder-dependent platform that creates subscription-based intermediation between organizations and activists, contradicting all three core criteria of free access, direct practitioner benefit, and platform independence.

While the platform appears free to use and serves individual homeowners, it lacks open source commitment, depends on institutional partnerships, and doesn't explicitly challenge extractive intermediaries in the energy sector.

While partially open source and free for public sector use, this government-to-government infrastructure tool primarily benefits institutional efficiency rather than individual practitioners, with no evidence of removing access barriers for marginalized communities or reducing platform dependence.

While Objector.ai empowers individual citizens against institutional planning processes, its closed-source subscription model and lack of free tier contradict the evaluator's core values of open access and anti-extraction.

While OCP promotes transparency in government contracting, it primarily serves institutional actors (governments and large organizations) rather than individual practitioners, relies on government partnerships rather than bypassing them, and its tools are only partially open source.

While OpenCRVS is genuinely open source and serves critical civil registration needs, it primarily benefits government institutions rather than individual practitioners, and its funding model relies heavily on traditional development partners rather than demonstrating platform independence.

OpenOrigins fails all three criteria as a proprietary, venture-funded platform that serves media organizations rather than individual practitioners, with closed-source technology that creates new dependencies rather than removing barriers.

While Open Ownership promotes transparency in corporate structures, it primarily serves governments and institutions rather than individual practitioners, operates through traditional funding models dependent on major foundations, and focuses on strengthening existing regulatory frameworks rather than providing direct tools to communities.

While OpenSanctions provides partial open access to sanctions data, it primarily serves institutional compliance needs through a hybrid subscription model rather than empowering individual practitioners, and its integration with financial surveillance systems contradicts anti-extraction principles.

OPORA scores moderately as a civic monitoring organization that directly serves citizens and election observers (Criterion 2: 15/20) but lacks open-source tools and relies heavily on international donor funding rather than providing free access to technology (Criterion 1: 10/20, Criterion 3: 10/20), with a small positive modifier for its decade-plus track record and policy engagement.

While Organise empowers individual workers against institutional power, its proprietary platform model, corporate funding (including Unilever Ventures), and lack of open-source architecture contradict Frederick's core values of free access, platform independence, and anti-extraction design.

While oTree is open-source and serves individual researchers, it primarily benefits academic institutions and government partners rather than directly empowering practitioners or communities outside institutional frameworks.

Open source climate data platform scores moderately on access (15/20) but serves primarily organizations rather than individual practitioners (5/20) with unclear platform independence (10/20), though limited dossier evidence constrains assessment.

A subscription-based, proprietary platform serving well-resourced professionals contradicts all three core criteria: it creates access barriers through paywalls, primarily benefits institutional actors over individual practitioners, and operates as a centralized commercial service rather than promoting independence from corporate platforms.

While GOV.UK Pay is partially open source and improves citizen payment experiences, it primarily serves government institutions rather than empowering individual practitioners, and reinforces rather than bypasses existing payment infrastructure dependencies.
